title: Izanagi and Izanami
paragraphs: In the beginning, the Kojiki says, heaven and earth were not yet divided. Among the early kami were Izanagi, 'the male who invites', and his sister Izanami, 'the female who invites'. The heavenly kami gave them a jewelled spear, Amenonuhoko, and sent them to shape the drifting land. Standing on the floating bridge of heaven, they lowered the spear and stirred the brine. When they lifted it, drops fell from the tip and became the first island, Onogoro.

They walked around a sacred pillar, spoke their vows, and their union produced the islands of Japan and many kami of sea, wind, mountain and field. But when Izanami gave birth to Kagutsuchi, the fire kami, the flames consumed her and she went to Yomi, the shadowy land of the dead. Izanagi, grieving, followed her there. At the gate she begged him not to look upon her, but he broke that promise. He lit a torch and saw that her form had changed. Ashamed and angry, she called the hags of Yomi after him.

Izanagi fled, holding back his pursuers with a magic comb, and escaped by rolling a great boulder across the pass between the worlds. There they spoke their final words, and the boulder sealed the road between the living and the dead. Polluted by the journey, Izanagi bathed in the river at Awagihara. As he washed, kami were born from his garments and his body: Amaterasu from his left eye, Tsukuyomi from his right, and Susanoo from his nose.

The Nihon Shoki tells the same outline with different names for the first islands and different words at the parting. Shinto purification rites still recall Izanagi's bath, and the story is passed on as one inherited telling among several.
themes: the boundary between life and death

title: The Sun and the Storm
paragraphs: Among the children of Izanagi were three who would shape the world: Amaterasu, the sun, born from his left eye; Tsukuyomi, the moon, from his right; and Susanoo, the storm, from his nose. Izanagi gave the sea and the storms to Susanoo, but the young kami was restless, weeping and raging by turns, and his father sent him away from the high plain of heaven.

Susanoo went to Takamagahara to take leave of his sister Amaterasu. She met him in armour, suspecting no good, and he swore an oath of goodwill. Yet his grief turned to wildness. He broke down the banks between the rice paddies, filled in the irrigation ditches, and let a horse loose in the sacred weaving hall, where a weaver was hurt. To the kami of heaven these were not small pranks but attacks on the order of the fields and the loom.

Amaterasu was grieved, and she withdrew into a rock cave. The world lost its light, the rice fields darkened, and the kami, alarmed, gathered at the riverbed of heaven to consider what to do. In some tellings it is this withdrawal, and not Susanoo's earlier misdeeds alone, that finally moves the heavenly kami to act.

Tsukuyomi, meanwhile, kept apart from his sister. One old account says that at a feast the moon kami struck down Ukemochi, the kami of food, and that Amaterasu, appalled, vowed never again to face him; this is why day and night are divided. The Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki give different reasons for the rift, and local shrines tell it differently again.

title: The Cave of the Sun
paragraphs: When Amaterasu hid herself in the rock cave, the plain of heaven and the land below were left in darkness. The eight million kami gathered in the dry bed of the Amenokawa, the heavenly river, and asked one another how the sun might be brought back. They brought long-lived birds to sing and set up a sacred tree upon the riverbank.

On its branches they hung a great mirror, forged by the smith kami, and strings of magatama jewels. Then Ame-no-Uzume, a kami of mirth and dawn, turned over a tub and danced upon it, stamping and laughing until all the assembled kami roared with laughter. The noise carried into the cave.

Amaterasu, curious, opened the stone door a crack and called out that she was hidden, so why was there joy? Uzume answered that a new and greater kami had appeared. The mirror was held up, and Amaterasu saw her own radiance reflected there. Drawn forward by wonder, she stepped out, and light returned to the world.

The kami stretched a sacred rope, the shimenawa, across the cave mouth so that she would not hide again, and the mirror was later said to have been taken to her shrine at Ise. The story is told as an explanation of the mirror, of the sacred rope and of the joyful festivals that honour the sun. Versions of the dance and the mirror differ between the Kojiki, the Nihon Shoki and regional shrines.

title: Susanoo and the Serpent
paragraphs: Sent away from heaven, Susanoo descended to the province of Izumo. There he met an old couple, Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi, and their daughter Kushinada-hime, all three weeping beside the river. Each year, they said, the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi came down from the mountains and demanded a young woman. Seven daughters had already been taken, and Kushinada was next.

Susanoo asked for Kushinada's hand and promised to save her. He turned her into a fine comb that he tucked into his hair, then had the old couple brew strong sake and set out eight vats of it on a platform behind eight gates. The serpent came, one head pushing through each gate, and drank. Its heads sank into the vats, and the creature slept.

Susanoo drew his sword and cut the serpent apart. The heads and the great body fell, and the river carried the creature away. In one of the tails he found a blade of extraordinary hardness that the serpent had carried, and he named it Kusanagi, 'grass-cutter', and sent it up to Amaterasu.

Kushinada became his wife, and he built a palace at Suga. There, looking over the land, he composed a poem about eight clouds rising over Izumo, often called the first Japanese poem. The sword Kusanagi later became one of the three sacred treasures, and the shrines of Izumo keep the memory of the couple and of the serpent's defeat.

title: The White Rabbit of Inaba
paragraphs: Ōkuninushi, a kami of Izumo, is remembered in the Kojiki as a builder of the land. Long before he ruled there, his many elder brothers set out across the country, all hoping to marry the princess Yakami of Inaba, and they made him carry their bags.

On the road along the Inaba coast they found a rabbit lying stripped of its fur and in pain. The brothers, amused, told it to bathe in salt water and dry itself in the wind, which only made it worse. Ōkuninushi, arriving later, asked what had happened. The rabbit explained that it had wanted to cross from the island of Oki to the mainland and had asked the crocodiles of the sea to line up for a race, counting them as it hopped across, and that it had mocked them at the last moment.

The last crocodile had seized it and torn away its fur. Ōkuninushi told the rabbit to wash in fresh water and roll in the yellow pollen of the cattails by the shore. The rabbit's fur grew back, and, grateful, it told him that he, not his brothers, would win Yakami-hime. And so it happened: the princess chose the kind younger brother.

The story is often read as a lesson in kindness and quick wit, and the hare is honoured in Izumo, where an old shrine by the sea is called Hakuto, 'the white rabbit'. Versions differ; the Nihon Shoki and some local tellings give the creatures other names and make the journey differently.

title: The Descent of Ninigi
paragraphs: When Amaterasu judged that the islands were ready for a ruler, she chose her grandson Ninigi-no-Mikoto. She gave him three treasures: the mirror that had drawn her from the cave, the string of magatama jewels, and the sword Kusanagi that Susanoo had taken from the serpent. These were to be the signs of his authority, and they are still called the three sacred treasures.

Ninigi and his companions came down from the high plain of heaven to the peak of Mount Takachiho in Kyushu. At the eight crossroads they met a kami of enormous stature whose radiance lit the road in both directions. The travellers stopped, unsure whether the stranger was friend or threat. Ame-no-Uzume spoke to him, and he named himself Sarutahiko Ōkami, kami of the crossroads.

Sarutahiko said he had come to lead the heavenly grandchild to his new land, and he went before them as guide. In some tellings he stayed to guard the roads afterward, and travellers still honour him at shrines by paths and junctions.

Ninigi ruled from a palace in the land of Hyūga and married Konohanasakuya-hime, the blossom princess. Their descendants, in the court's telling, were ancestors of Emperor Jimmu, the legendary first emperor. The Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki use the descent to link the imperial line to the sun kami, which is part of why these chronicles were compiled; older local traditions preserve other accounts.
